explanation:
# Connector assembly: translating pieces so their red plugs meet

This explanation follows the supplied reference program. I have checked the placements below against the two demonstration grids by hand-computed shifts. I have **not** executed the program on the query inputs, so what I say about the queries is an expectation, not a measured result.

## What the input is made of

Each input contains several solid-coloured **pieces** and many single red cells (colour 2). Every red cell touches one piece, usually at the tip of an arm or on one flank. These red cells act as **connectors**. One piece is a solid yellow (colour 4) block, and it is the **anchor**. In both demonstrations it occupies exactly the same cells in the output as in the input. Every other piece moves to a new place.

## What the output does, checked on demonstration 1

**The anchor.** The yellow 3×3 block at rows 11–13, columns 9–11 has four connectors:
- (10,9) and (10,11) above it,
- (12,12) to its right,
- (14,10) below it.

**Cyan (8).** Its body is at rows 1–3, columns 15–19. It has four reds: (0,15), (0,19), (4,16) and (4,18). The output moves it by (+6, −7).
- Its two lower reds go to (10,9) and (10,11), exactly the yellow top connectors.
- Its upper reds land at (6,8) and (6,12), where they become new open sockets.

**Green (3).** Its body is at rows 18–19, columns 1–5. Its reds are (20,1) and (20,5), four columns apart, the same spacing as cyan's upper connectors. It is moved by (−14, +7), so (20,1)→(6,8) and (20,5)→(6,12). Green therefore docks on top of cyan.

**Blue (1).** It has four connectors: (3,4), (4,8), (5,2) and (7,8). It is moved by (+9, +8).
- (3,4)→(12,12), yellow's right connector.
- (5,2)→(14,10), yellow's bottom connector.
- (4,8)→(13,16) and (7,8)→(16,16) become new sockets.

**Grey (5).** Its reds are (15,15) and (18,15). It is moved by (−2, +1), so they land on (13,16) and (16,16), the two remaining blue sockets.

Two red cells that meet merge into one cell. That is why the red count falls from 16 to 8. When the assembly is finished, every connector is paired. Pieces are only translated: they are never rotated or recoloured. Pieces never overlap one another.

## Demonstration 2 shows the same pattern

The yellow block's connectors are (10,11), (10,12), (12,9) and (12,13).

- **Blue (1)** has reds (12,2), (12,4), (15,6) and (17,4). It is shifted by (−5, +5).
  - (15,6)→(10,11) and (17,4)→(12,9), both yellow connectors.
  - (12,2)→(7,7) and (12,4)→(7,9) become new sockets.
- **Magenta (6)** has reds (6,16) and (6,18). It is shifted by (+1, −9), so they land on (7,7) and (7,9).
- **Green (3)** has reds (10,16), (10,19), (13,16) and (15,17). It is shifted by (−3, −4).
  - (13,16)→(10,12) and (15,17)→(12,13), both yellow connectors.
  - (10,16)→(7,12) and (10,19)→(7,15) become new sockets.
- **Cyan (8)** has reds (20,9) and (20,12). It is shifted by (−13, +3), so they land on (7,12) and (7,15).

## Turning the rule into a procedure (the reference program)

1. **Split the grid into pieces and connectors.** Pieces are the 4-connected components of cells that are neither background nor red. Each red cell is assigned to the piece at the smallest Manhattan distance. A tie raises an error.
2. **Choose the anchor.** The anchor is the largest piece made entirely of colour 4. Its connectors form the initial set of open sockets.
3. **Search with backtracking.** For each unplaced piece, try every translation that puts one of its reds on an open socket. A placement is rejected if:
   - any cell of it falls outside the grid,
   - its body overlaps occupied cells, open sockets or closed sockets,
   - its reds land on occupied or closed cells.

   Every red of the piece that lands on an open socket closes that socket. All its other reds become new open sockets. Placements that match more sockets are tried first; this lets blue in demonstration 1 plug into two yellow connectors at once. Failed partial states are memoised.

   The search returns the **first** assembly that places every piece and leaves no socket open. It does not count alternative solutions, so I make no claim that the solution is unique.

   Pieces with a single connector are supported, for example the small green pole in query 2.

   The program computes a direction set ("normal") for each connector, but these are **not** used to accept or reject placements. Matching is purely positional. I kept them only to leave the working code unchanged.
4. **Render.** Start from a blank background canvas. Stamp the anchor, then each piece at its shift together with its reds. A checkpoint is emitted after each piece is stamped.

## The query inputs: pieces and connectors read off the grids, placements not executed

**Query 1.** There are 24 reds and 7 pieces.

| Piece | Location | Connectors |
|---|---|---|
| Yellow 4×5 anchor | rows 11–14, cols 9–13 | (10,9), (11,14), (14,8), (15,10) |
| Large cyan | rows 1–4, cols 16–22 | (0,22), (1,23), (3,16), (4,21) |
| Small cyan U | rows 2–3, cols 10–12 | (1,10), (1,12) |
| Maroon (9) | rows 6–9, cols 3–7 | (8,3), (9,4), (10,5), (10,7) |
| Blue | rows 10–13, cols 18–23 | (9,19), (9,22), (14,18), (14,23) |
| Green | rows 20–23, cols 1–6 | (20,4), (21,6), (24,2), (24,5) |
| Orange (7) bar | row 21, cols 12–17 | (20,12), (20,17) |

I expect the search to chain these pieces outward from the yellow connectors. I have not run it here, so I cannot report the exact shifts.

**Query 2.** There are 22 reds and 7 pieces.

| Piece | Location | Connectors |
|---|---|---|
| Yellow 3×3 anchor | rows 10–12, cols 10–12 | (9,12), (10,9), (12,13), (13,11) |
| Cyan | rows 1–5, cols 3–6 | (0,3), (1,7), (3,7), (5,6), (6,3) |
| Magenta | rows 4–6, cols 18–22 | (3,18), (3,22) |
| Green pole | rows 11–13, col 4 | (14,4) only |
| Grey | rows 11–14, cols 18–23 | (15,19), (15,22) |
| Blue | rows 19–23, cols 2–6 | (19,4), (20,2), (24,2), (24,6) |
| Large green | rows 20–24, cols 11–17 | (20,12), (20,15), (21,10), (23,10) |

The same assembly procedure applies. Again, the actual placements are unexecuted expectations.
